newsitem.title: USA: US solid waste industry seen consolidating further.
newsitem.headline: US solid waste industry seen consolidating further.

text.p: Allied Waste Industries Inc's purchase of Laidlaw Inc's solid waste business is part of a larger trend toward consolidation in the solid waste industry as companies jockey for position in a rapidly changing marketplace.
"The theme in the waste industry, for years, has been consolidation," said James Kelleher, analyst at Argus Research. "You will see an ongoing continuation of acquisitions."

On Wednesday Allied Waste agreed to buy Laidlaw's solid waste business in a deal valued at $1.5 billion, making the Scottsdale, Ariz.-based company the nation's fourth-largest solid waste company with annual 1996 revenues of $1 billion.
The deal is just the latest in a long line of acquisitions as companies improve efficiency.

"If you're operating an integrated disposal collection company you've got to have access to capital and if you've got market share and low cost capital it's a real advantage in the industry," said William Fisher analyst at Raymond James.

Kelleher said the industry could accomplish the same efficiency that Blockbuster achieved when it set up a national chain of video stores and similar moves being attempted in the second-hand auto market by firms like AutoNation and Car Max.

"You can indeed realize a lot of efficiencies with a national approach," he said. "The same can be true for garbage." Another factor that should spur consolidation is the rapidly changing enviormental attitudes of municipalities. With the U.S. becoming more and more "green" regulations are become more costly to implement.

"If you're an independent garbage hauler and you're running a litle dump where you just dump the trash, in the future you're going to have to do things like methane collection and clay lining of pits ... you'll need some money," Kelleher said.
With those sort of expenses likely to increase in the coming years "mom & pop" operators may find it more attractive to sell out to larger companies seeking acquisitions.
With most of the big acquisitions already done those small independent acquisitions will likely take center stage.
Another area for potential acquisitions is municipal garbage operations.
"There is a zillion little towns out there that do their own garbage hauling and some big cities too," Kelleher said pointing to New York City as a prime example.
"USA Waste, United Waste Systems Inc and Browning-Ferris Industries Inc are all slugging it out in the New York City market to try and push out those old (private) cartel companies," Kelleher said.
"There is a great deal of room to privatize because trash service (has been) one of the bastions of municipal life in this country," he said.
